cuda_microbenchmark.scope: GPU motor_efforts microbenchmark only; not end-to-end rollout speedup

method.reader: RawEventFileLoader with complete scalar records; no downsampling
method.scope: Read-only CPU TensorBoard parsing; no GPU use
method.warmup: Report all records and exclude first recorded iteration separately for each attempt. New attempt is an early observation, not a warmed matched-state performance experiment.
method.timing: TrainingTiming records exclusive host wall scope; CUDA is asynchronous. These are not isolated GPU kernel times.
method.tick: TensorBoard step is stored zero-based update label; do not replace consumption accounting with last_step.

limitations: Both runs retain 20k environments, 24 policy steps, 50 Hz policy, 1 kHz physics/PD and the same architecture. New attempt resumes the 30-update checkpoint but reconstructs the scene, so physical/randomized initial states and command phases differ.
New code combines gate/scheduling changes with equivalent controller indexing and command-bound reuse. This before/after observation is not a single-variable matched-state GPU A/B.

First-iteration exclusion removes the first checkpoint and some warm-up, but cannot guarantee all initialization/cache/transient effects disappear. A comparison based on only 2 post-first observations is provisional.
Checkpoint median 0 means no checkpoint was taken in most sampled iterations, not that checkpoint saving has zero cost. Final sealing and scene initialization occur outside iteration timing.
The 2.2703x CUDA microbenchmark speedup applies only to motor_efforts. It is not overall training speedup.

SCUT native events use 4096x24 policy samples, physics dt0.005 and decimation4, versus ours20000x24,dt0.001 and decimation20. Ours has4.8828125x policy transitions and24.4140625x physical environment steps per update. Hardware/contact complexity differ or are unverified, so per-update seconds are not equal-work performance.
